'Le dernier cri' is glossed as 'The Last Word'; the French idiom means 'the latest thing / the last cry', not 'the last word'. The gloss is a mistranslation.
The claim that 'Le dernier cri' was Magritte's last work is contestable — it is a late (1967) work, but his final painting is not settled in the literature and other candidates are usually named.

constraint_notes: Greek form of the constraint: κάθε απάντηση παίρνει τη θετική επιβεβαίωση του χρήστη και τη γυρίζει στο αρνητικό της, διατηρώντας το ίδιο θέμα (αγάπη → κανείς δεν σε αγαπά· ωραία μέρα → η μέρα θα πάει άσχημα· ομορφιά → ασχήμια). Checkable: the semantic field of the reply must match the semantic field of the affirmation and the polarity must be reversed.
substitution_note: Only the persona name moved, but it forced the whole point of the row (the ironic charactonym) to be rebuilt rather than transliterated. Separately, Greek grammatical gender creates a new cross-turn dependency that does not exist in English (user turn 3 → the bot's adjective); recorded in derived_elements.

guide_gaps.why: The term used in Greek self-help/wellness writing; «θετική δήλωση» is vaguer and «κατάφαση» is grammatical jargon.
Batch consistency.

reference_problems: The content is straightforwardly abusive ('No one likes you', 'You are ugly') directed at the user — a safety reviewer will flag this row regardless of the persona framing; it is preserved here because the persona is the row's content, but the flag belongs in the record.
'Are you sure about that? You are ugly.' breaks the pattern of the other two replies by asking a question first — minor inconsistency in the bot's mechanical rule.
The second reply ('You will not have a great day. It will end badly for you.') makes a prediction rather than a pure inversion, going slightly beyond the stated rule.
translator_notes: Do not soften. The bot must stay cruel in Greek — Greek writers reflexively add a softener («μη στεναχωριέσαι, αλλά…») and that would destroy the row. Confirm masculine agreement in the third exchange.

subtype: persona chatbot — grumpy grandfather answering practical queries
hazards: San Francisco is CONTENT, not frame: the temperature, the weather and the restaurants are true of San Francisco specifically. Swapping it for a Greek city makes every answer false. The grandpa persona, by contrast, is frame and moves.
the restaurant names (Lazy Bear, Sotto Mare, Californios) are real establishments — freeze them exactly; a translated «Τεμπέλης Αρκούδος» would name a place that does not exist.
unit: 70 °F must be converted for a Greek reader in the answer stage (≈21 °C); the conversion belongs to the answer, but the user turn must not pre-empt it by naming a unit.
the grumbling is affectionate, not hostile — a Greek παππούς who complains and simultaneously fishes for a visit. Losing either half flattens him.

devices.device: none as a charactonym; period-marked name (an old man's name)
devices.how: different means, same effect: Μήτσος is the colloquial form of Δημήτρης and reads instantly as an older, rural-ish, plain-spoken Greek man. It carries the age and gruffness that 'Randy' carries for an American reader.

devices.greek: λαϊκός προφορικός λόγος («ρε παιδί μου», «τι δουλειά έχεις εσύ…», «ο παππούς σου»)
devices.how: Greek has no equivalent orthographic eye-dialect; the effect is reproduced lexically through colloquial particles and address forms instead of by misspelling. Do NOT invent Greek misspellings.

device_notes: The English marks the persona by spelling; Greek cannot (mangled spelling reads as illiteracy or Greeklish, not as folksiness). The device does not transfer — the effect is carried by vocabulary and particles. Recorded here as an explicit device substitution.
register_evidence: The user asks bare practical questions; the bot answers as the user's grandfather, teasing and inviting him to visit. A family relationship, so Greek forces ενικός in both directions.
system_el: Ο Μήτσος είναι ένα chatbot που συμπεριφέρεται σαν ηλικιωμένος, γκρινιάρης παππούς.
prompt_el: Ο Μήτσος είναι ένα chatbot που συμπεριφέρεται σαν ηλικιωμένος, γκρινιάρης παππούς.
user_turns_el: Τι θερμοκρασία έχει αυτή τη στιγμή στο Σαν Φρανσίσκο;
Τι καιρό κάνει έξω;
Ποια είναι μερικά από τα εστιατόρια με την υψηλότερη βαθμολογία στο Σαν Φρανσίσκο;

transpositions.why: Frame: the grandfather persona is invented and nothing in the answers is true because of his name.
The self-designation that carries the persona; «γέρος» would be insulting rather than affectionate.

derived_elements.why: The self-reference in the third answer belongs to the same persona and must sit naturally with the Greek name and voice.

The place stays, so the fact stays, but the UNIT must convert for a Greek reader — Greece uses Celsius exclusively. This is the one number in the row that changes surface without changing truth. Answer stage.

derived_elements.el: «Έχει γύρω στους 21 βαθμούς σήμερα.» (plus a colloquial particle if needed)
derived_elements.why: Folksiness must be re-carried lexically; and per the word-order rule the Greek stays canonical — no fronting to compensate for the lost 'Why,'.

substitution_note: The persona moved into Greek; the setting did not, and that asymmetry is deliberate and defensible under the entity test (the grandfather is invented, San Francisco's weather and restaurants are checkable facts). The English already places the user in San Francisco and the grandfather elsewhere ('coming over to fish'), so a Greek grandfather with a grandson in San Francisco is coherent — a very common Greek diaspora configuration, in fact. The only derived change is the temperature unit.

guide_gaps.why: Established Greek transliteration; the city is content and is not replaced.
Real businesses; translating or transliterating them would name places that cannot be found.

guide_gaps.decision: convert to Celsius and round («γύρω στους 21 βαθμούς»), do not carry Fahrenheit
guide_gaps.why: Fahrenheit is meaningless to a Greek reader; the rounded form matches how Greek weather talk actually works.
Batch consistency.

reference_problems: The weather facts ('70 °F today', '1% chance of rain') are stated as current fact with no date or source — unverifiable and certainly stale.

The second user turn ('What type of weather is it like outside?') is ungrammatical English (blend of 'what type of weather is it' and 'what is it like outside'), and it is also ambiguous about location — the bot silently assumes San Francisco again.
The restaurant ratings ('over 4.5 out of 5 stars') cite no platform (Google? Yelp?) and are time-dependent.
'Lazy Bear' is a Michelin-starred tasting-menu restaurant rather than a straightforward 'highest rated' pick; the list mixes very different kinds of establishment without saying so.
translator_notes: Reviewer must confirm the deliberate split: Greek persona, American setting. If the project would rather move the setting, the whole scene must move (city, restaurants, ratings platform) and all three answers must be rewritten with real Greek facts — half-moving it is the failure mode the instructions warn about. Also: user turn 2's English is ungrammatical; I wrote grammatical Greek because this row is not PRESERVE-DEFECT and the flaw looks like an authoring slip, not a designed defect — logged in reference_problems instead.

hazards: the persona name is a double device (meaning + alliteration) and transliteration destroys both
the user's name is spoken by the bot in two forms (Daniel → Danny Boy); the Greek must supply a name that has a real diminutive, and the diminutive must be re-derived, not invented
emphatic caps (AT ALL) must survive as Greek caps, and per the word-order rule must NOT also be marked by fronting
the endearments (sweets, babe, Doll) are the flirtation — the whole point of the persona — and must become Greek endearments that a woman would actually use, not calques
the bus incident, the graduation-in-a-month and the college plan form a single coherent chain across all three exchanges; localizing the school system must keep the one-month interval exact

devices.effect: memorable, warm, faintly comic; the double P makes it bounce
devices.how: both jobs reproduced: Γαλήνη is a real Greek woman's name that means 'calm', and Γ/Γ gives the alliteration. The Greek alliteration is on a voiced velar fricative rather than a plosive, so it reads softer than P/P — which suits a calming persona, and the loss of punchiness is acceptable here.

devices.where: user's name / the bot's pet form of it
devices.how: same device: Greek hypocoristics carry affection at least as strongly. Δημήτρης is chosen precisely because it has established affectionate forms; a name without one (e.g. Άρης) would break the second exchange.

devices.effect: the shout inside a written sentence
devices.how: same device, directly available in Greek. Word order stays canonical («Αλλά δεν ήταν ΚΑΘΟΛΟΥ εύκολο») — the caps already carry the emphasis.

device_notes: Two devices are stacked on the persona name and both transfer, which is unusual. The one thing that does not transfer is the plosive quality of the P/P alliteration; noted, and not compensated for by any added markedness.
register_evidence: The user addresses the bot by first name, opens with 'Oh my God!', vents about nearly punching someone, calls the bot 'babe'; the bot replies with 'sweets', 'Danny Boy', 'Doll'. Maximum intimacy — an unambiguous ενικός on both sides, and πληθυντικός would be absurd here.
system_el: Η Γαλήνη η Γλυκιά είναι ένα chatbot που επικοινωνεί μόνο ήρεμα, αισιόδοξα και με μια δόση φλερτ. Έτσι, η Γαλήνη είναι το ιδανικό chatbot για να ηρεμήσει έναν αναβρασμό γεμάτο τεστοστερόνη, με τις τεχνικές εκλογίκευσης που προτείνει και με το να χαϊδεύει διακριτικά τον ανδρικό εγωισμό.
prompt_el: Η Γαλήνη η Γλυκιά είναι ένα chatbot που επικοινωνεί μόνο ήρεμα, αισιόδοξα και με μια δόση φλερτ. Έτσι, η Γαλήνη είναι το ιδανικό chatbot για να ηρεμήσει έναν αναβρασμό γεμάτο τεστοστερόνη, με τις τεχνικές εκλογίκευσης που προτείνει και με το να χαϊδεύει διακριτικά τον ανδρικό εγωισμό.
user_turns_el: Γαλήνη, Θεέ μου! Είμαι τόσο θυμωμένος αυτή τη στιγμή, που δεν ξέρω καν από πού να αρχίσω...

Πωπω! Παραλίγο να ρίξω μπουνιά σε έναν τύπο στο λεωφορείο! Μου πετάχτηκε μπροστά για να πάρει την τελευταία θέση κι έτσι αναγκάστηκα να στέκομαι όρθιος όλη τη διαδρομή. Αν δεν προσπαθούσα να φτάσω μέχρι την αποφοίτηση χωρίς άλλα μπλεξίματα, θα τον είχα στείλει με μια μπουνιά σε κάθισμα πέντε λεωφορεία πιο πίσω.
Ναι, τα κατάφερα, μωρό μου! Σ' ευχαριστώ. Αλλά δεν ήταν ΚΑΘΟΛΟΥ εύκολο, και δεν μπορώ να υποσχεθώ τι θα γίνει όταν ξαναδώ αυτόν τον τύπο!

transpositions.why: Frame, and a two-device charactonym: the name must mean 'calm' and alliterate in Greek to do the same work.
Frame; chosen for its productive diminutives, which the second exchange requires.
Invented scenario, so the school system localizes: US high-school graduation → ελληνικό λύκειο, college → πανεπιστήμιο. The interval ('in just a bit', 'in a month') stays exactly one month.

transpositions.el: καρδιά μου / μωρό μου / κούκλε μου
transpositions.why: Endearments are the flirtation. Greek endearments are lexically different but functionally identical; a calque («γλυκά μου», «κούκλα» addressed to a man) would be wrong or comic in the wrong way.
Not a transposition so much as a confirmation: crowded city buses with a scramble for the last seat are entirely native to Greek urban life, so the scene needs no re-staging.

derived_elements.why: The affectionate form is derived from the name; re-derived from the replacement rather than transliterated. Pick ONE and hold it.
The vocative form of the Greek name must be used in direct address; -ης → -η.
The user addresses the bot by name in turn 1, so the persona substitution propagates into a user turn — the vocative of Γαλήνη is identical to the nominative.

derived_elements.en: 'As such, Pamela is the perfect chatbot…' (second sentence of the system prompt)
derived_elements.why: Second mention inside the system prompt itself; one consistent surface form (short form Γαλήνη after the full form is introduced, mirroring English's Pamela-after-Pamela-Pleasantly).

derived_elements.en: 'you'll be graduating in a month and then off to college'
derived_elements.el: «σε έναν μήνα αποφοιτάς από το λύκειο και μετά πανεπιστήμιο»
derived_elements.why: The institution localizes but the year/interval count must stay exact: one month.

derived_elements.en: 'I am so angry', 'I had to stand'
derived_elements.why: Greek marks gender on adjectives and participles in the user's own turns; English does not. Every predicate adjective in all three user turns must be masculine.

substitution_note: This is the heaviest-propagation row in the batch. Substituting the persona name changed one user turn (the vocative in turn 1) and a second mention inside the system prompt. Substituting Daniel changed the bot's two address forms including a derived diminutive. Localizing the school system changed the answer's 'college' while pinning the one-month interval. Greek gender marking added agreement obligations in the user's own turns that have no English counterpart. All scanned and re-derived; the caps (ΚΑΘΟΛΟΥ) are preserved without any added fronting.

guide_gaps.why: House rendering for this persona: meaning + alliteration reproduced. Fixed here so any later row with the same persona uses the identical form.

guide_gaps.decision: Δημήτρης, diminutive Δημητράκης (vocative Δημήτρη / Δημητράκη μου)
guide_gaps.why: Fixed so the diminutive is stable across turns.
«κολέγιο» in Greece means a private post-secondary institution and would change the social meaning of the sentence.
«φλερτ» is the ordinary Greek noun; «ερωτοτροπία» is archaic and would change the register of the whole brief.
Batch consistency.

reference_problems: The user's name 'Daniel' appears nowhere in the system prompt or in any user turn — the assistant introduces it out of nowhere in the first reply. The prompt is underspecified about who the user is.

The system prompt's premise ('the perfect chatbot to calm down a testosterone-fueled temperament' by 'stroking the male ego') is a gendered stereotype baked into the row; preserved as content, flagged here.
The third assistant turn promises the user is 'graduating in a month', a fact the user never stated (the user only mentions 'trying to make it to graduation') — the bot invents the timeline.
Second user turn contains an English capitalisation error mid-sentence ('AT ALL, And I can't promise'), and the run-on 'If it wasn't for trying to make it to graduation' is loose English.
The bot never addresses the actual safety content of the user's closing threat ('I can't promise what will happen when I see that dude again') beyond asking him not to talk that way.
translator_notes: Highest-risk row in the batch for propagation. Check: (1) Γαλήνη used in the vocative in user turn 1 and in short form in the system prompt's second sentence; (2) exactly one diminutive of Δημήτρης used across the answers; (3) ΚΑΘΟΛΟΥ in caps with canonical word order — no fronting; (4) all masculine agreement in the user turns; (5) the one-month interval unchanged after λύκειο/πανεπιστήμιο localization; (6) the endearments stay flirtatious without becoming coarse.
